channel.description: Recent content in Units on Athenaeum

item.title: Allegory
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. Allegory gives visible bodies and actions to abstractions. The unit asks when this clarifies moral experience and when it makes that experience stranger or more disturbing.

Visual plan. A four-work comparison of personification, moral journey, temptation, and symbolic landscape.

Artworks and Images

Allegorical Images

1 / 1

Looking at the Images

Giotto’s Justice and Injustice make moral conditions visible as opposed forms of government. Justice sits frontally beneath balanced architecture while ordered communal life unfolds below; Injustice occupies a damaged fortress while violence and disorder appear at his feet.

item.title: Art and Empire
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. Representation can turn foreign people, places, ruins, and histories into objects of knowledge, fantasy, display, or possession. The unit asks who is entitled to represent whom.

Visual plan. A four-part argument: reconstructed antiquity, intimate Orientalist encounter, staged ethnographic fantasy, and the violence underlying imperial commerce.

Artworks and Images

Empire, Display, and Possession

1 / 1

Looking at the Images

Designed under Owen Jones and photographed by Philip Henry Delamotte, the Egyptian Court transforms antiquity into a reconstructed environment for metropolitan spectators. Delacroix’s interior depends upon access to a space presented as private and foreign; Gérôme’s polished surface makes an invented scene look documentary. Turner’s Slave Ship sacrifices descriptive clarity to color and storm in order to confront imperial commerce as catastrophe.

item.title: Art and the Reformation
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. Sacred and mythological events are displaced into ordinary landscapes, work, weather, and public life while religious conflict makes images themselves objects of suspicion.

Visual plan. A five-image argument. Three Bruegel works establish sacred or mythic meaning submerged in ordinary reality; Holbein intensifies the problem of bodily incarnation; Hogenberg supplies the historical crisis surrounding religious images.

Artworks and Images

Sacred History in an Ordinary World

1 / 1

item.title: Chivalric Romance
item.description:
Artworks and Images

Romance and the Grail

1 / 1

Looking at the Images

The ivory mirror case turns courtship into a playful siege: armed lovers attack a “castle” defended by women, converting desire into the vocabulary of chivalric combat.

item.title: Courtly Life
item.description: The Tale of Genji is “a classic work of Japanese literature written by the noblewoman, poet, and lady-in-waiting Murasaki Shikibu around the peak of the Heian period, in the early 11th century. It is the first novel written by a woman to have won global recognition.”

item.title: Cubism
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. Cubism rejects the stable viewpoint and reconstructs objects through planes, fragments, signs, and multiple perspectives. The unit must also confront the colonial framework within which European artists appropriated African forms.

Visual plan. A five-image sequence from Cézanne’s restructuring of bodies and space through proto-Cubism, analytic Cubism, collage, and the movement’s more legible public form.

Artworks and Images

The Development of Cubism

1 / 1

item.title: Dada and Surrealism
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. Dada attacks the cultural authority of art after the war; Surrealism seeks another order in dream, chance, desire, and the unconscious. They belong in one unit but should remain visibly distinct.

Visual plan. A six-work survey divided explicitly into Dada and Surrealism. Duchamp’s readymade is restored to its historical Dada context.

Artworks and Images

I. Dada and Anti-Art

1 / 1

II. Surrealist Dream

1 / 1

item.title: Devotional Grief
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. Devotional art does not simply depict sacred suffering. It trains the beholder to participate emotionally through bodily pose, gesture, composition, repetition, and direct address.

Visual plan. Van der Weyden is the principal close-reading object. A smaller comparison gallery places it between Byzantine icon, Giotto’s narrative lamentation, and Michelangelo’s sculpture.

Featured Artwork

Devotional Grief: Before and After

item.title: Elegy and Memory
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. The unit introduces apostrophe, ritual address, remembrance, and the limitations of memorial art.

Visual plan. A two-work comparison between private familial remembrance and public civic memorial.

Artworks and Images

Greek Funerary Memorials

1 / 1

Looking at the Images

The two stelai use the same funerary medium for very different kinds of remembrance:

item.title: Gothic Art and Pilgrimage
item.description:
Artworks and Images

Sacred Space and Pilgrimage

1 / 1

Looking at the Images

Move through this sequence spatially. Autun’s tympanum places judgment above the church entrance; Chartres then expands the sculptural threshold into a complete architectural environment of portals, vertical ascent, colored light, and processional movement. The pilgrim badge reduces a great shrine to a small object that could be worn and carried home.

item.title: High Renaissance to Mannerism
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. Students first see Renaissance pictorial order established and then watch that order strain, lengthen, twist, and become deliberately artificial.

Visual plan. A six-image transition gallery. Uccello establishes constructed pictorial order; Raphael gives its mature ideal; Michelangelo places that ideal under pressure; Pontormo, Parmigianino, and Bronzino make distortion and artificiality unmistakable.

Artworks and Images

From Renaissance Order to Mannerist Distortion

1 / 1

item.title: Impressionism and Pointillism
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. Impressionism treats perception as fleeting and situated; Pointillism attempts to organize that fleeting perception through optical theory and method.

Visual plan. A five-part transition from atmospheric impression and modern social scenes to Seurat’s systematic reconstruction of sensation.

Artworks and Images

From Impression to Optical System

1 / 1

Looking at the Images

Monet’s broken brushwork makes sunrise inseparable from the act of seeing it. Morisot treats figures, reflections, clothing, and water with an airy incompleteness; Degas uses cropping and social distance to make modern leisure feel uncomfortable rather than festive.

item.title: Lyric and Desire
item.description:
If Homer and Virgil presented the heroic, the epic, the historical, the mythological … and Keats and Rilke contemplated enigmatic objects of classical art and described their effects on the observer, Sappho gives us the intensely personal, the inner experience, the seemingly private — almost as if overheard.

Fragment 31

item.title: Modernism
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. Modernist difficulty becomes a response to historical rupture, cultural overload, broken traditions, and competing voices rather than an arbitrary refusal to communicate.

Visual plan. A restrained four-object sequence. Poetry should dominate the page; the visual material demonstrates editorial fracture, simultaneous text and image, and two paths into abstraction.

Featured Artwork

Fragmentation and Abstraction

1 / 1

item.title: Motion and Machine
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. Artists attempt to invent forms adequate to trains, automobiles, crowds, repeated movement, industrial force, and urban simultaneity. The unit also examines the dangerous conversion of speed and violence into aesthetic ideals.

Visual plan. A nine-image movement survey divided into three sections: the photographic analysis of movement, Italian Futurism, and parallel experiments outside Futurism.

Artworks and Images

I. Recording Movement

1 / 1

The Founding and Manifesto of Futurism

Futurism announced itself not merely as a new artistic style but as an assault on inherited habits of thought. Marinetti praises danger, machinery, speed, aggressive action, and the modern industrial city. He presents the motorcar, locomotive, factory, steamship, and aeroplane as emblems of a world whose movement has rendered older standards of beauty obsolete.

item.title: Nature as Revelation
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. Nature becomes more than external scenery or overwhelming force. It appears as memory, symbol, moral presence, sacrament, or evidence of a reality perceived through imaginative attention.

Visual plan. A three-work progression from observed landscape to visionary landscape and explicitly symbolic creation.

Artworks and Images

Observed and Visionary Nature

1 / 1

Looking at the Images

Constable’s landscape grounds vision in observed weather, labor, water, and local place. Palmer makes the rural world denser and more visionary: moon, tree, field, and human figure seem charged with inward significance. Blake’s geometrical creator turns the act of measuring the universe into a symbolic image.

item.title: Neoclassicism and Revolution
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. Antiquity becomes a public language through which artists and writers imagine aristocratic dignity, civic virtue, sacrifice, revolution, and political legitimacy.

Visual plan. A four-image transition from Rococo private pleasure through Grand Manner elevation to republican virtue and revolutionary martyrdom.

Artworks and Images

From Rococo Pleasure to Revolutionary Virtue

1 / 1

Looking at the Images

Fragonard’s secluded garden, suspended slipper, and billowing surfaces make Rococo pleasure feel private, weightless, and knowingly theatrical. Reynolds uses classical quotation and monumental pose to elevate a living actress into the figure of Tragedy.

item.title: Paradise Lost
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. Milton attempts to write sacred epic without relying upon Catholic image, ceremony, or mediation. The central problem is whether poetic magnificence can remain obedient to the religious truth it claims to serve.

Visual plan. A focused two-image reception study. Blake should illuminate Milton rather than turn the page into a general gallery of Fall imagery.

Artworks and Images

Blake Illustrates Milton

1 / 1

item.title: Philosophical Poetry
item.description:
On Socrates

Greek Anthology 7.96, attributed to Diogenes Laertius

Drink now, Socrates, in the house of Zeus.
Truly a god called you wise,
and Wisdom herself is divine.
From the Athenians you received only hemlock;
but they drank it themselves through your mouth.

Against the Fear of Death

item.title: Post-Impressionism
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. Post-Impressionism is not one uniform style but a retrospective name for several different departures from Impressionism. Seurat makes perception systematic; Cézanne reconstructs form; Gauguin flattens observed reality into symbolic design; Van Gogh turns color and brushwork toward emotional and spiritual intensity. The unit then follows those intensifications toward Expressionism without misclassifying Van Gogh, Ensor, or Munch as members of German Expressionism proper.

Visual plan. The existing five-work gallery moves from Post-Impressionism to a concise Fauvist coda. A two-work bridge then presents Ensor and Munch as precursors to Expressionism, followed by Kirchner’s Street, Berlin as a representative work of the movement itself.

item.title: Postwar Poetry and Abstraction
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. The course concludes by asking what poetry and painting can still make present after narrative certainty, traditional symbolism, and stable representation have been reduced or abandoned.

Visual plan. A deliberately spare four-work progression from geometric reduction through gesture, color field, and quiet postwar grid.

Artworks and Images

From Reduction to Abstraction

1 / 1

Looking at the Images

Mondrian reduces painting to vertical and horizontal relations, primary color, and unequal balance. Pollock makes the record of bodily movement spread across the whole field. Rothko slows the encounter into hovering color and uncertain depth, while Martin’s grid replaces dramatic gesture with minute repetition and attention.

item.title: Revolution and Realism
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. Realist art gives monumental attention to workers, poverty, travel, collective action, and ordinary bodies. The unit asks what happens when art rejects elevated historical or mythological subjects.

Visual plan. A four-image transition from revolutionary allegory to labor and ordinary social experience.

Artworks and Images

From Revolution to Realism

1 / 1

Looking at the Images

Delacroix still organizes revolution through allegory: Liberty is both a woman in the crowd and a larger-than-life public symbol. Courbet refuses that elevation, giving laborers monumental scale without heroic narrative. Millet similarly enlarges repetitive agricultural work, while Daumier compresses class, fatigue, and anonymity into a railway carriage.

item.title: Sturm und Drang
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. Feeling, genius, and rebellion become claims against inherited restraint. The unit forms the transition from Enlightenment order to Romantic intensity.

Visual plan. A three-image transition from Enlightenment experiment to irrational pressure and nightmare.

Artworks and Images

From Enlightenment Experiment to Nightmare

1 / 1

Looking at the Images

Wright’s experiment presents Enlightenment inquiry as a drama of light, spectatorship, and moral unease. Fuseli turns the sleeping body into a stage for forces that reason cannot govern. Goya’s sleeping draftsman produces monsters while the instruments of rational labor lie unused.

item.title: Symbolism and the Fin de Siècle
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. Art loosens its obligation to describe ordinary reality. Atmosphere, dream, music, myth, eroticism, and decorative form become means of suggesting what cannot be stated directly.

Visual plan. Whistler is the principal close-reading object. A three-work gallery follows it from atmospheric near-abstraction into erotic myth and dream imagery.

Featured Artwork

Symbolist Myth and Dream

1 / 1

item.title: The Baroque
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. Baroque art and metaphysical poetry use shock, movement, theatricality, violent address, and bodily experience to make spiritual realities present.

Visual plan. A three-work comparison of revelation through light, sculpture as sacred theatre, and bodily movement on a monumental scale.

Artworks and Images

Sacred Drama in Baroque Art

1 / 1

Looking at the Images

Caravaggio makes conversion arrive through a beam of light and a barely perceptible pointing hand within an otherwise ordinary room. Bernini dissolves the boundary between sculpture, architecture, hidden lighting, and theatre. Rubens converts the raising of the Cross into a diagonal struggle of coordinated bodies.

item.title: The Dutch Golden Age
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. Dutch painting invests rooms, objects, professions, bodies, and ordinary light with sustained attention. The unit asks what moral or spiritual meaning can survive without overt sacred spectacle.

Visual plan. A three-work comparison of domestic judgment, public knowledge, and mortality embodied in objects.

Artworks and Images

Observation and Mortality

1 / 1

Looking at the Images

Vermeer suspends a domestic action between material detail and moral judgment: the woman, the scales, the pearls, and the Last Judgment behind her create a network of possible meanings without fixing a single lesson. Rembrandt presents knowledge as public performance, arranging the surgeons around an opened body and a commanding lecturer.

item.title: The Modern City
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. Railways, boulevards, crowds, bridges, advertisements, and anonymity create a new rhythm of perception. The city becomes both spectacle and estrangement.

Visual plan. A four-image city sequence: enclosure beside the railway, the station itself, the boulevard pedestrian, and the illuminated city viewed from above.

Artworks and Images

Urban Experience

1 / 1

Looking at the Images

Manet places the modern railway just beyond an iron barrier, making steam, enclosure, and interrupted looking more important than a descriptive view of the train. Monet enters the station and lets smoke fracture its architecture. Caillebotte gives the rebuilt boulevard a startling breadth while preserving the isolation of individual pedestrians.

item.title: The Renaissance Lyric
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. The sonnet turns inherited formal constraints into a theatre for desire, beauty, time, self-presentation, and frustrated argument.

Visual plan. A two-work comparison between mythic idealization and courtly self-fashioning.

Artworks and Images

Beauty and Self-Fashioning

1 / 1

Looking at the Images

Botticelli stages beauty and desire through an elaborate mythological procession whose figures are bound together by repeated gestures, flowing contours, and a densely cultivated garden. Hilliard compresses courtly self-presentation into a portrait miniature: costume, pose, roses, motto, and tiny scale make the sitter appear at once displayed and privately possessed.

item.title: The Romantic Hero
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. Romanticism makes the isolated, defiant, historically burdened individual into a central poetic and visual figure. The unit distinguishes heroic self-fashioning from genuine solitude and catastrophe.

Visual plan. A three-work comparison of manufactured public heroism, solitary spectatorship, and national suffering personified.

Artworks and Images

Heroism, Solitude, and Historical Burden

1 / 1

Looking at the Images

David’s Napoleon is a manufactured public image: wind, gesture, inscriptions, and the rearing horse turn political authority into heroic destiny. Friedrich’s wanderer is seen from behind, so the viewer partly occupies his position while remaining unable to read his face.

item.title: The Sublime
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. The sublime names an encounter with what exceeds ordinary measure: ocean, mountain, darkness, catastrophe, violence, or apparently infinite power.

Visual plan. A three-work comparison of destruction, emptiness, scale, and human smallness.

Artworks and Images

Terror, Scale, and Astonishment

1 / 1

Looking at the Images

Friedrich’s Sea of Ice nearly eliminates the human subject beneath splintered, thrusting masses. Monk by the Sea reverses the density: a minute figure faces an almost empty expanse. Turner fills the scene with storm, snow, violence, and historical catastrophe until stable form begins to dissolve.

item.title: Victorian Medievalism and Classical Revival
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. Nineteenth-century artists reconstruct medieval and classical worlds in response to industrial modernity. The past becomes a source of beauty, moral gravity, fantasy, confinement, and critique.

Visual plan. A four-work gallery divided between medieval revival and classical revival. The limited selection prevents the unit from becoming a general Victorian-art anthology.

Artworks and Images

The Recovered Past

1 / 1

Looking at the Images

The Pre-Raphaelite works recover literary and medieval subjects through painstaking surfaces, saturated color, and symbolic detail. Yet the recovered past is not secure: Millais’s Ophelia is beautiful at the moment of death, while Hunt’s Lady is trapped between art, desire, and the world outside her mirror.

item.title: Why Paint at All?
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. Photography changes the meaning of likeness, evidence, memory, and artistic labor. Painting must now make a new claim for what it can do.

Visual plan. A four-image sequence from the earliest surviving photograph to photography’s increasing command of detail and time, concluding with Courbet’s large allegorical claim for painting.

Featured Artwork

Photography and Painting

1 / 1

item.title: World War I
item.description:
Unit plan

Purpose. The mechanical force celebrated by the avant-garde encounters industrialized war. Heroic rhetoric, bodily integrity, stable perspective, and confidence in civilization all become difficult to sustain.

Visual plan. A five-image sequence moving from Expressionist psychological fracture to machinery, ruined landscape, gas warfare, and prophetic animal catastrophe.

Artworks and Images

War and the Shattered Image

1 / 1

Looking at the Images

Kirchner’s amputated hand is imagined rather than documentary, but it makes psychic damage visible before the soldier has physically lost the limb. Nevinson organizes gunners and machine into a single hard mechanism. Nash lets the ruined landscape indict the optimistic title, while Dix reduces the attacking soldiers to masked, advancing instruments.
